extracted.subtask_description: Prove and reason about convergence/divergence of infinite series (via partial sums and standard tests) and compare cardinalities of sets (bijections, countability, Cantor arguments). Typical textbook-chapter tasks and exercises for introductory proof-based mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of an infinite series via partial sums
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinite series ∑_{k=1}^∞ a_k converges to S if its sequence of partial sums s_n (where s_n = a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_n) converges to S. If the sequence of partial sums does not converge to a finite number (or the sum does not make sense), the series diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sequence of partial sums s_1, s_2, s_3, ... and apply the definition of convergence of sequences (ε–N formulation, Definition 13.5). Text emphasizes this is the principal definition (Definition 13.7) though in practice one uses convergence tests. Exercises ask to apply the definition directly to prove tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric series criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A geometric series a + ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ··· (with a, r ∈ R) converges to a/(1−r) if |r| < 1. If a ≠ 0 and |r| ≥ 1, the geometric series diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 13.10 illustrates with a = r = 1/2; derive a neat closed form for partial sum s_n (e.g., via algebraic manipulation 2s_n − s_n) to show s_n → a/(1−r) when |r|<1. Exercise 1 in the section asks to prove this using the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison test (for series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose (a_k) and (b_k) are sequences with 0 ≤ a_k ≤ b_k for each k. If ∑ b_k converges then ∑ a_k converges. Conversely, if 0 ≤ b_k ≤ a_k for each k and ∑ b_k diverges, then ∑ a_k diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as an exercise to prove using partial sums and monotonicity. This is a basic test used in calculus for comparing positivity-bounded series to known convergent/divergent series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit comparison test (exercise-formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose a_k and b_k are series with a_k, b_k > 0 for each k. If lim_{k→∞} (a_k / b_k) = 0 and ∑ b_k converges, then ∑ a_k converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text presents this as an exercise (with permission to use earlier exercises). Note: the standard full limit-comparison test also treats the case when the limit is a positive finite number; the book asks to prove a stated version as an exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute convergence test
rubrics_metrics.description: If the series ∑ |a_k| converges, then the series ∑ a_k converges (i.e., absolute convergence implies convergence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an exercise to prove possibly using the Comparison Test or other exercises. This is a standard result used to establish convergence of conditionally/non-conditionally convergent series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio test
rubrics_metrics.description: For a series with positive terms (a_k > 0), if L = lim_{k→∞} (a_{k+1} / a_k) and L < 1 then ∑ a_k converges; if L > 1 then ∑ a_k diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as an exercise; proof may use geometric series comparison. The exercise allows using prior results. (The text phrases the test in the usual ratio-test form and asks the reader to prove it.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of a convergent series must tend to zero (Theorem 13.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∑_{k=1}^∞ a_k converges (to some S), then the sequence (a_n) converges to 0 (i.e., a_n → 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved directly from the convergence of partial sums: a_n = s_n − s_{n−1}, and since s_n → S and s_{n−1} → S, their difference tends to 0. The contrapositive gives a divergence test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence test (corollary)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sequence a_n does not converge to 0 (or converges to a nonzero number), then the series ∑ a_k diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a simple initial test to show divergence; the text underscores it only detects divergence, not convergence. Examples provided where a_n → 0 but the series still diverges (e.g., harmonic series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonic series divergence example
rubrics_metrics.description: The harmonic series ∑_{k=1}^∞ 1/k diverges (sums grow without bound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: grouping terms up to 2^n shows s_{2n} ≥ 1 + n/2, which → ∞ as n → ∞. This illustrates that a_n → 0 is not sufficient for convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of cardinalities via bijection (Definition 14.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets A and B have the same cardinality (|A| = |B|) if there exists a bijective function f : A → B. If no bijection exists, |A| ≠ |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition applies to finite and infinite sets. Examples: explicit bijections are used to show |N| = |Z| and |(0,1)| = |R| (via composition arguments). The text emphasizes that finding any single bijection suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countable / countably infinite / uncountable definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is countably infinite if |N| = |A| (there exists a bijection N → A). A set is countable if it is finite or countably infinite. A set is uncountable if it is infinite and there is no bijection N → A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation: |N| = ℵ_0 (aleph-naught). Examples: Z and Q are countably infinite; R is uncountable. Exercises ask to produce explicit bijections or listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countably infinite iff elements can be listed (Theorem 14.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is countably infinite if and only if its elements can be arranged in an infinite list a_1, a_2, a_3, ... that includes every element of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a practical technique: demonstrate countability by giving an explicit enumeration/listing (often via an array and a snaking path for Q). Conversely, a listing induces a bijection from N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonal argument (no surjection N→R / R uncountable)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any purported function f : N → R (writing decimals of f(n)), construct a real number b whose nth decimal differs from the nth decimal of f(n); then b is not in the image of f, so no surjection exists and R is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives explicit construction: choose b's nth decimal 0 if f(n)'s nth decimal ≠ 0, else 1. This method produces a number differing in every diagonal place, proving the non-surjectivity of any f: N→R. This is the canonical proof of Theorem 14.2 showing |N| ≠ |R|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing bijections between common sets (technique/examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show equality of cardinalities by explicitly constructing bijections (e.g., f(n)=−n matching finite sets, enumerations matching N↔Z, geometric bijection f(x)=x/(x+1) mapping (0,∞)→(0,1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text: bijection N→Z given by a table; bijection (0,∞)→(0,1) via projection/similar triangles yielding f(x)=x/(x+1); compose bijections and use transitivity of |A|=|B| for proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of |A| < |B| and |A| ≤ |B| (Definition 14.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: |A| = |B| iff there is a bijection A→B. |A| < |B| means there is an injection A→B but no bijection A→B. |A| ≤ |B| means there is an injection A→B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extends the notion of 'less than' to infinite cardinalities. Example: injection N→R shows |N| ≤ |R|; Cantor's theorem shows strict |N| < |R|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's theorem: power set strictly larger (|A| < |P(A)|)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set A there is an injection A → P(A) but no surjection A → P(A); hence |A| < |P(A)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs injection f(x) = {x} and uses the diagonal set B = {x ∈ A : x ∉ f(x)} to show no function A→P(A) can be surjective. This yields an infinite ascending chain of larger cardinalities via repeated power sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product of countable sets is countable (Theorem 14.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are countably infinite, then A × B is countably infinite (i.e., can be listed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: write A and B as lists and follow a path through the grid (snake/diagonal) to enumerate A×B. Corollary: finite Cartesian products of countable sets are countable (induction). Exercise: explicit bijection for N×N→N (e.g., pairing function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of two countable sets is countable (Theorem 14.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are countably infinite, then A ∪ B is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a shuffled list a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2, ... (omitting duplicates) to enumerate the union. This gives a practical method for combining enumerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite subset of a countably infinite set is countably infinite (Theorem 14.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is countably infinite and A ⊆ B is infinite, then A is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: traverse an enumeration of B and select elements that belong to A to produce an infinite listing for A. Useful for proving countability of subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncountable subset forces containing set uncountable (Theorem 14.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If U ⊆ A and U is uncountable, then A is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if A were countable, then an infinite subset U of A would be countably infinite (Theorem 14.8), contradicting U uncountable. Use this to deduce uncountability by finding an uncountable subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation ℵ0 for cardinality of naturals
rubrics_metrics.description: The cardinality of the natural numbers N is denoted ℵ0 (aleph-naught). Any countably infinite set has cardinality ℵ0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout to compare cardinalities (e.g., ℵ0 < |R|). This is a definitional notation rather than a test.
